chapters.n: Jude, brother of James and so likely a half-brother of Jesus, humbly calls himself Christ’s servant. He writes to believers who are called, loved by the Father, and kept safe in Christ.

f.g: Greek Ioudas — the same name as Judah or Judas.

chapters.n: He wishes them mercy, peace, and love in abundance.
Jude planned to write about the salvation they share, but felt urged instead to call them to fight for the faith God gave the Saints once for all.

f.g: Struggle hard, like an athlete or wrestler.

chapters.n: Some ungodly men have slipped in unnoticed. They twist God’s grace into an excuse for immorality and deny Jesus Christ, our only Master and Lord.

f.w: turning the grace of our God into lasciviousness

chapters.n: Jude reminds them of history: the Lord saved Israel from Egypt, yet later destroyed those who refused to believe.
Angels who abandoned their proper place and position are held in darkness for the great day of judgment. Latter-day Saints connect “first estate” to premortal life.
Sodom, Gomorrah, and nearby towns gave themselves to sexual immorality and perverse desires, and their fiery destruction stands as a warning.

f.g: Unnatural or other flesh—gross sexual perversion.

chapters.n: In the same way, these intruders, relying on their “dreams,” defile their bodies, reject authority, and insult glorious beings.

f.g: Perhaps claiming visions to justify their behavior.

chapters.n: Even Michael the archangel, disputing with the devil over Moses’s body, didn’t dare insult him but said, “The Lord rebuke thee.” This story comes from a Jewish tradition outside the Old Testament.

f.g: Latter-day Saints identify Michael as Adam.

chapters.n: These men mock what they don’t understand, and the things they know only by animal instinct are what destroy them.
Woe to them! They follow three Old Testament villains: Cain the murderer, Balaam who served for profit, and Korah who rebelled against Moses.

f.g: Korah, who led a rebellion against Moses and Aaron.

chapters.n: Jude piles up images: hidden reefs at the Saints’ love feasts, rainless clouds, fruitless trees uprooted and doubly dead.

f.g: Love feasts—shared meals of early Christians, often with the sacrament.

chapters.n: They are like wild waves foaming up their shame, and like wandering stars that drift off course into eternal darkness.

f.g: Planets or meteors that don’t keep a fixed place—an image of unreliable guides.

chapters.n: Enoch, seventh from Adam, prophesied about such people: the Lord will come with countless holy ones. Jude quotes a Jewish book attributed to Enoch; Latter-day Saints have more of Enoch’s prophecies in the book of Moses.
He will judge everyone and convict the ungodly of all their ungodly deeds and harsh words against Him. The repeated word “ungodly” hammers the point.
These men grumble and complain, follow their own desires, boast loudly, and flatter people to gain an advantage.
But you, dear friends, remember what the Apostles of the Lord Jesus Christ foretold.
They warned that in the last time mockers would come, driven by their own ungodly desires.
These people cause divisions; they follow natural instincts and do not have the Spirit.
Instead, build yourselves up on your most holy faith and pray in the Holy Ghost.
Stay in God’s love as you wait for the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ that leads to eternal life.
Show mercy to those who are wavering, treating each person’s situation with care.

f.g: Distinguishing between cases; some manuscripts read ‘on those who doubt.’

chapters.n: Rescue others as if snatching them from fire. Show mercy, but carefully—hating even clothing stained by sin.

f.w: pulling them out of the fire

chapters.n: Jude ends with a famous blessing: God is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you blameless before His glory with great joy.
To the only God, our Savior, belong glory, majesty, power, and authority, now and forever. Amen.
